risk_changes.before: In 2025, the U.S. government announced a series of tariffs, including tariffs targeting a broad range of imports and targeted tariffs on goods from specific countries and industries. In response, many countries imposed reciprocal tariffs and other trade restrictions on the United States. Although many of these tariffs, countermeasures and other trade restrictions have since been eased or paused, their initial announcements triggered considerable volatility in global markets and heightened economic uncertainty, and the global trade situation, particularly between the United States and China, continues to be highly dynamic. Further, throughout 2025 the U.S. government has initiated numerous investigations into products and industries under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962. For example, in April 2025, the Department of Commerce launched an investigation into the national security impacts of imported semiconductors and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. While the results of this investigation remain unknown, it is expected to result in additional tariffs and trade restrictions that may adversely impact our business. Similar investigations on other industries or products, including automotive, copper, steel, aluminum, critical minerals and aircraft, may also adversely impact the semiconductor industry and our business. These changes have, and similar changes in the future may continue to, increase the cost or reduce the availability of raw materials and supplies we need to operate, cause customers to advance, delay, reduce, or cancel orders, shift buying patterns, impact demand in our end markets, complicate demand forecasting for us and our customers, increase supply chain complexity and contribute to volatility, a broader economic slowdown or recession. Any of these impacts or changes could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

Although many of these tariffs, countermeasures and other trade restrictions have since been eased or paused, their initial announcements triggered considerable volatility in global markets and heightened economic uncertainty, and the global trade situation, particularly between the United States and China, continues to be highly dynamic. These actions have, and similar actions in the future may continue to, increase the cost or reduce the availability of raw materials and supplies we need to operate, cause customers to advance, delay, reduce or cancel orders, shift buying patterns, impact demand in our end markets, complicate demand forecasting for us and our customers, increase supply chain complexity and contribute to volatility, a broader economic slowdown or recession. risk_changes.before: The markets for semiconductor products are cyclical, and increased production may lead to overcapacity and lower prices, and conversely, we may not be able to satisfy unexpected demand for our products.

The cyclical nature of the semiconductor industry has resulted in periods when demand for our products has increased or decreased rapidly. The demand for our products may vary based on market conditions in our major end markets. Demand in these end markets can fluctuate significantly based upon, for example, consumer spending, consumer preferences, the development of new technologies and macroeconomic conditions, including impacts related to tariffs and other trade restrictions. If we overbuild inventory in a period of decreased demand, or we expand our operations and workforce too rapidly or procure excessive resources in anticipation of increased demand for our products, and that demand does not materialize at the pace at which we expect, or declines, our operating results may be adversely affected as a result of underutilization of capacity, charges related to obsolete inventory, asset impairment or inventory write-downs, increased operating expenses or reduced margins. For example, we have experienced, and may in the future experience, periods of customer inventory adjustments and other customer behaviors that may adversely affect our operating results. Further, any capacity expansions by us or other semiconductor manufacturers could also lead to overcapacity in our target markets which could lead to price erosion that could adversely impact our operating results. Conversely, during periods of rapid increases in demand, our available capacity may not be sufficient to satisfy the demand. In addition, we may not be able to expand our workforce and operations in a sufficiently timely manner, procure adequate resources and raw materials, locate suitable third-party suppliers or respond effectively to changes in demand for our existing products or to demand for new products requested by our customers, and our current or future business could be materially and adversely affected.

risk_changes.after: The semiconductor industry is cyclical, and we may be unable to satisfy increases in demand for our products or, conversely, may build capacity and inventory in excess of demand, which could lead to overcapacity, lower prices and reduced margins.

Demand in our end markets also depends on capital spending by our customers and their end customers, the pace and durability of which are uncertain and could be affected by, among other factors, industry-wide capacity additions; lower-than expected end-user adoption of, or returns on investment in, new technologies; export controls or other trade restrictions; and broader corrections in market valuations. Any of these factors could cause customers to delay, reduce or cancel deployments or orders, or pause purchases while they absorb installed capacity or inventory. For example, the growth of AI technologies and related infrastructure has driven, and is expected to continue to drive, demand in certain industries that we serve, but the timing and amount of that demand can change significantly and rapidly as a result of the factors described above, as well as factors specific to AI, such as constraints on electric power, land, cooling and construction resources, including state and local restrictions aimed at limiting or preventing new data center construction; and changes in the economics of AI model training and inference. Accordingly, our recent revenue growth, including growth attributable to any particular end market or application, should not be relied upon as an indicator of future results.

Our future success significantly depends on our ability to execute our business strategy, continue to innovate, improve our existing products and design, develop, produce and market innovative new products and system-level solutions. As part of our strategy, we are continuing to move beyond individual components and toward more sophisticated, integrated solutions that sense, interpret and act on data from the physical world, which we refer to as Physical Intelligence. Our solutions increasingly combine analog, mixed-signal and power technologies with digital processing, embedded software and machine learning, and are often delivered as subsystems and system-level platforms. Product design, development, innovation and enhancement are complex, time-consuming and costly, require significant research and development investment and may not generate a return. These risks are heightened for more complex, software-intensive and AI-enabled solutions, which typically require more complex development cycles, larger upfront investment, broader ecosystems of partners and capabilities in areas such as software engineering, data science, systems architecture and cybersecurity, where we have less experience and face intense competition for talent. There can be no assurance that we will be able to develop and introduce new and improved products in a timely or efficient manner or that new and improved products, if developed, will achieve market acceptance.

Our products generally must conform to various evolving and sometimes competing industry and regulatory standards, which may adversely affect our ability to compete in certain markets or require us to incur significant costs. In addition, our customers generally impose very high quality and reliability standards on our products, which often change and may be difficult or costly to satisfy. Any inability to satisfy customer quality and reliability standards or comply with industry and regulatory standards and technical requirements may adversely affect demand for our products and our results of operations.

In addition, a portion of our revenue depends on investment in AI infrastructure, including data center and automated test equipment applications, which is driven largely by the capital spending of hyperscale data center operators, AI silicon developers and their contract manufacturers. These customers may qualify alternative suppliers, internally develop capabilities that our products currently provide or adopt power, optical, control or other data center architectures in which our products have reduced content. In addition, AI data center expansion faces growing public, political and community opposition over electricity costs and reliability, water and land use, environmental impacts and public subsidies, which could lead to restrictions, higher costs, reduced incentives, litigation or project delays and cancellations, and cause our customers to reduce, delay or redirect infrastructure spending. Any of these developments could reduce demand for our solutions and adversely affect our revenue and growth. If we are unable to successfully execute our strategy, we may not realize the expected return on the significant investments we are making, and our business, financial condition and results of operations could be adversely affected.

To remain competitive, we have invested in or acquired, and may continue to invest in or acquire, other companies, purchase or license technology from third parties, or enter into other strategic transactions in order to introduce new products or enhance our existing products.

An element of our business strategy involves expansion through the acquisitions of businesses, assets, products or technologies that allow us to complement our existing product offerings, diversify our product portfolio, expand our market coverage, increase our engineering workforce, expand our technical skill sets or enhance our technological capabilities. For example, in July 2026 and November 2026, respectively, we completed our acquisitions of Empower Semiconductor and Alif Semiconductor to expand our capabilities in AI-related markets, including AI compute power delivery and AI-enabled edge processing. We may not be able to identify businesses in the future that have the technology or resources we need and, if we find such businesses, we may not be able to invest in, purchase or license the technology or resources on commercially favorable terms or at all. Acquisitions, investments and technology licenses are challenging to complete for a number of reasons, including difficulties in identifying potential targets, the cost of potential transactions, competition among prospective buyers and licensees, the need for regulatory approvals, and difficulties related to integration efforts. In addition, investments in companies are subject to risk of a partial or total loss of our investment. Both in the United States and abroad, governmental regulation of acquisitions, including, for example, antitrust and other regulatory reviews and approvals, has become more complex, increasing the costs and risks of undertaking, and may prevent us from consummating, significant acquisitions. Many companies have sufficient financial, manufacturing, technical, sales and marketing resources to develop and market products that compete with our products. Some of our competitors may have more advantageous supply or development relationships with our current and potential customers or suppliers. Our competitors also include both emerging companies selling specialized products in markets we serve and companies outside of the United States, including entities associated with well-funded efforts by foreign governments to create indigenous semiconductor industries. From time to time, governments around the world may provide incentives or make other investments that could benefit and give competitive advantages to our competitors. For example, in August 2022, the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 (CHIPS Act) was signed into law to provide financial incentives to the U.S. semiconductor industry. Government incentives, including any that may be offered in connection with the CHIPS Act, may not be available to us on acceptable terms or at all. Further, such programs typically require companies to adhere to various performance obligations, which we may not achieve. If our competitors can benefit from such government incentives and we cannot, it could strengthen our competitors’ relative position and have a material adverse effect on our reputation and business.
